title: The CIA Sabotage Manual for Product Organizations
author: Leading in Product
summary: Writing for product leaders, Benedikt Kantus borrows the 1944 OSS manual on simple sabotage and shows how closely its prescriptions describe ordinary product organisations. His claim is that nobody is deliberately sabotaging anything, but the effect is the same: decisions slow, good people leave and momentum dies quietly through meetings, approvals and committees. He catalogues the behaviours at four levels: the meeting room (approval multiplication, committee capture, relitigating settled decisions), the manager's chair (perfectionism on the wrong things, promoting the loudest rather than the most effective), individual contributors (strategic slowness, skill hoarding, fake compliance), and the culture (watermelon reporting, rewarding heroics over prevention, deliberate vagueness). The remedy is modest but demanding: give the behaviours names so the room can recognise them, then ask honestly which of them you are doing now because the organisation rewards it.
points: Most organisational sabotage looks like due diligence, stakeholder alignment and responsible governance, which is why it goes unseen.
Approval multiplication, committee capture and reopening settled decisions slow product teams without anyone intending harm.
Managers sabotage through perfectionism on low-value work and by promoting the loudest rather than the most effective people.
Culture-level damage, such as watermelon status reports and rewarding 2am heroics over prevention, drives the best people out before leaders notice.
Naming the behaviours creates shared vocabulary, and the harder second step is asking which of them you are doing yourself.
quotes: That is the uncomfortable part. Not that someone is deliberately sabotaging your product org. Almost certainly, nobody is.
The effect is the same whether the sabotage is intentional or not. Decisions slow to a crawl. Good people burn out and leave.
The conference table is where most organizational sabotage takes place. It does not look like sabotage. It looks like due diligence, stakeholder alignment, and responsible governance.
Management dysfunction is harder to spot. It wears the costume of leadership. These behaviors feel like rigor and accountability.
Promoting the loudest PM rather than the most effective one, then wondering why team dynamics deteriorate quarter after quarter.
Celebrating the PM who heroically shipped at 2am while ignoring the PM who prevented the crisis through good planning three weeks earlier.
The OSS manual worked because these behaviors are invisible from the inside. They feel normal. They feel careful.
Naming them is the first move. Not to assign blame. To create a shared vocabulary for what is actually happening.
